title: Who runs the grid — and can they upgrade it in time?
label: 22 October 2026 · Upgrading the grid
summary: The Committee questioned senior officials from the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero (DESNZ), the regulator Ofgem and the National Energy System Operator (NESO) about delivering a major upgrade of Britain’s electricity transmission network by 2030. Witnesses agreed the investment is necessary and that failure would be costly, but described serious risks: planning delays, supply-chain pressure, complex technical work to change parts of the live system, and unclear public visibility of progress. The Department says it is accountable and is building stronger delivery and engineering capacity; Ofgem says it has tightened incentives and penalties; NESO says it is improving system planning and operating the grid. MPs pressed for clearer, single place reporting, stronger consumer safeguards and an independent review of a recent near-miss on system security.

glossary.definition: Department for Energy Security and Net Zero, the ministerial Department that sets UK energy policy.
The UK regulator for gas and electricity markets, responsible for setting network price controls and incentives.
National Energy System Operator, the public corporation that plans and operates the electricity system in real time.
Payments made when the system cannot use cheaper electricity generation, so other, often gas, plants are run instead.
Accelerated Strategic Transmission Investment, Ofgem’s programme to speed up approval and funding of major grid upgrades.
Technology on power lines that lets operators safely carry more electricity by measuring real-time conditions.
Nationally Significant Infrastructure Project — a planning process used for very large schemes.
A government-backed public company intended to be a new player in transmission and connections.

chapters.title: Who is accountable?
chapters.takeaway: DESNZ says it is ultimately accountable for policy and delivery oversight, while Ofgem regulates networks and NESO runs the system — but the split can feel confusing.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: We are examining the £70bn upgrade to the transmission network to reach 95% clean power by 2030. Please introduce your roles in two sentences.

turns.speaker: Jonathan Brearley
turns.text: I'm the Permanent Secretary at DESNZ; we set energy policy and oversee delivery of major programmes.

turns.speaker: Emily Bourne
turns.text: I'm Director for Electricity Systems and Networks at DESNZ, focusing on planning and delivery of the grid work.

turns.speaker: Tim Jarvis
turns.text: I'm CEO of Ofgem. We regulate energy markets and networks and set incentives and penalties for delivery and cost.

turns.speaker: Beatrice Filkin
turns.text: I'm Ofgem's Director of Major Projects, responsible for regulating the big transmission upgrades and monitoring delivery.

turns.speaker: Fintan Slye
turns.text: I'm CEO of NESO. We plan the system over the long term and run the electricity system in real time from the control room.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Who is accountable if these projects are not delivered by 2030 and the lights are at risk?

turns.speaker: Jonathan Brearley
turns.text: The Department is ultimately accountable for policy and oversight. Transmission companies are responsible for delivery; Ofgem regulates and NESO operates the system.

turns.speaker: Rupert Lowe
turns.text: With so many organisations involved, I'm worried no one will actually be accountable. I'd like an independent engineering review of a recent near-miss on 23 June.

turns.speaker: Tim Jarvis
turns.text: We take system security very seriously. Ofgem has launched a detailed investigation and uses in-house and independent engineers. We published an interim report and will continue examining the evidence.

turns.speaker: Fintan Slye
turns.text: NESO has given Ofgem all the data. We support the review and have our own independent experts looking at operations. We also published a separate report on whistleblowing culture and are acting on recommendations.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Parliament will want clarity. Will you produce a single, clear account of who does what and where responsibility lies?

turns.speaker: Jonathan Brearley
turns.text: Yes. We'll set out roles and responsibilities clearly in upcoming policy documents and the strategic planning products, and we'll write to the Committee on how we'll present that information.

chapters.title: The main barriers to delivering the upgrades
chapters.takeaway: Big projects take years; planning, consents, supply chain and the technical work of changing a live system are the chief risks to hitting 2030.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: There are 88 projects needed by 2030. What must be done to make sure they are delivered?

turns.speaker: Jonathan Brearley
turns.text: We must unlock finance, co-ordinate delivery, and oversee the whole portfolio so networks, Ofgem and NESO work together to align generation and grid upgrades.

turns.speaker: Tim Jarvis
turns.text: Upgrading transmission takes around eight to ten years for major projects. We introduced ASTI to speed approvals, an advanced procurement mechanism for supply chains, and stronger incentives.

turns.speaker: Rupert Lowe
turns.text: NESO said eight projects could be accelerated to reduce constraint costs; two years later they’re still scheduled after 2030. Were those recommendations realistic?

turns.speaker: Emily Bourne
turns.text: Some projects, including three in East Anglia (Norwich to Tilbury split into two, and the offshore Sea Link), could not be shifted to 2030 despite efforts — planning, supply chain and consenting remain big barriers.

turns.speaker: Rupert Lowe
turns.text: Which single barrier is the greatest threat?

turns.speaker: Emily Bourne
turns.text: Planning and consent risk is the hardest to remove. We are seeking land rights and other reforms, but some measures await parliamentary time.

turns.speaker: Fintan Slye
turns.text: A technical hurdle rising up the agenda is system access: when you connect or upgrade parts of the live transmission system you often must take sections offline, and that coordination becomes harder as more projects compete for access.

turns.speaker: Tim Jarvis
turns.text: We can use regulation to shift incentives, but some risks — like physical planning delays and global supply-chain pressures — are partly outside our control.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Should more of this be treated as a single nationally significant infrastructure programme rather than many separate projects?

turns.speaker: Beatrice Filkin
turns.text: Some of the biggest schemes are already classed as NSIPs. Transmission companies choose whether to pursue national DCOs or local consents; local engagement matters to reduce impacts on communities.

turns.speaker: Jonathan Brearley
turns.text: We will explain to the Committee how the NSIP criteria apply, but routing and local mitigation do require local handling, even if the overall programme is national.

chapters.title: Costs to consumers and constraint payments
chapters.takeaway: Not upgrading the grid would be costly: NESO’s current estimate of constraint costs is around £7–8 billion by 2030, but mitigations and updated planning may reduce that — transparency is needed.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: What are the estimated constraint costs by 2030 if projects slip?

turns.speaker: Fintan Slye
turns.text: Our clean power 2030 advice estimated constraint costs of roughly £7–8 billion if key projects can't be accelerated.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: That means paying generators not to run and using more expensive gas – is that right?

turns.speaker: Fintan Slye
turns.text: Yes. A big portion of those costs would be paying gas-fired plants to run while holding back wind or solar; the gas price heavily influences the bill impact.

turns.speaker: Anna Dixon
turns.text: The NAO considered an average saving of about £30 per consumer if some projects were accelerated. How confident are you in those figures?

turns.speaker: Tim Jarvis
turns.text: Numbers are sensitive to assumptions, particularly gas prices. The clear message is that consumers are better off by doing the upgrades than by not doing them.

turns.speaker: Anna Dixon
turns.text: What practical mitigations can reduce constraint costs beyond building new lines?

turns.speaker: Fintan Slye
turns.text: Short-term measures include rolling out dynamic line rating to squeeze more capacity from existing lines, better system access planning, and using flexible demand like data centres and storage more smartly.

turns.speaker: Beatrice Filkin
turns.text: Ofgem has increased delivery incentives and can penalise late delivery. We also require better transparency on project costs and plan to publish a state-of-the-market style report next year to show progress and impacts on bills.

turns.speaker: Anna Dixon
turns.text: Citizens Advice says it struggles to contest regulatory choices because of appeal risks. Will you consider removing appeal fee risks for consumer groups?

turns.speaker: Tim Jarvis
turns.text: Ofgem is committed to consumers. We understand the concerns about the appeals process and will work with the Department on options to ensure consumer voices are heard.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Committee wants one clear place to see project progress, costs and risks. Will you deliver a single, simple reporting product?

turns.speaker: Jonathan Brearley
turns.text: We'll provide that. We will bring together the strategic plan, NESO data and Ofgem reporting into a coherent narrative and confirm how we'll present it to Parliament.

chapters.title: Next steps: planning, capacity and governance
chapters.takeaway: Officials promised a stronger, joined-up strategic plan, more engineering and delivery capacity in the Department, better skill and supply-chain plans, and more transparency; MPs pressed for an independent review of the June incident.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: When will the Strategic Spatial Energy Plan and central network plan be published?

turns.speaker: Fintan Slye
turns.text: We have pathway options to 2050 with the Secretary of State; a formal public consultation and environmental assessment will run next year. The centralised network plan will follow and be on a three-year cycle.

turns.speaker: Anna Dixon
turns.text: That central plan in 2028 is late for the 2030 target. How do you reconcile near-term delivery needs with a long-term plan?

turns.speaker: Jonathan Brearley
turns.text: We have already started strategic planning through earlier holistic network work. The SSEP is part of an ongoing process to improve coordination; it won't be the first or only action.

turns.speaker: Rupert Lowe
turns.text: Do Ministers know whether energy security or net zero is the priority? It feels mixed.

turns.speaker: Jonathan Brearley
turns.text: The Government wants both. We aim for a diverse generation mix that delivers net zero while protecting security of supply and minimising costs.

turns.speaker: Rupert Lowe
turns.text: How will you increase in-house engineering and delivery skills in the Department?

turns.speaker: Jonathan Brearley
turns.text: DESNZ is becoming more of an infrastructure delivery Department. We're building engineering, major-projects and programme skills and will bring in the specialists needed to oversee delivery.

turns.speaker: Anna Dixon
turns.text: What about jobs and supply chain — how many roles and how will you train people?

turns.speaker: Beatrice Filkin
turns.text: Industry published a sector growth plan: network companies estimate up to around 210,000 additional skilled jobs by 2035; companies are coordinating apprenticeship and training plans and exploring joint training hubs.

turns.speaker: Chris Kane
turns.text: If a transmission company is clearly failing, can you step in ahead of a collapse and reassign work or use tougher regulatory measures?

turns.speaker: Tim Jarvis
turns.text: We have strong financial and enforcement powers and use them. We monitor projects from the start; if firms underperform they face penalties. It’s harder to simply transfer major projects, but mechanisms like GB Grid exist to add capacity over time.

turns.speaker: Rupert Lowe
turns.text: I remain unconvinced. I still want an independent technical review of the June near-miss. Will you consider commissioning one for Parliament?

turns.speaker: Tim Jarvis
turns.text: Ofgem has independent experts in its investigation and has published interim findings. We're open to discussing further transparency. If Parliament wants a separate independent review, that's a matter for Parliament to commission.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: We will include these asks in our Report. Please provide the Committee with the clear single reporting product promised and further detail on costs, the maintenance budget point raised, and the planned engineering capacity increases.

turns.speaker: Jonathan Brearley
turns.text: We will. We'll write with specifics on the maintenance figures and follow up on the other points you requested.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Thank you all. We will publish our Report and expect responses on the commitments made today.
